speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MADAME CHIANG KAI-SHEK ADDRESS TO MEMBERS OP THE SENATE AND OP THE HOUSE OF COMMONS TO BE PRINTED IN OFFICIAL REPORT OF DEBATES
speechtext:
I am sure the house will wish to have as part of the permanent records of its proceedings the historic address which was delivered in this chamber this morning by Madame Chiang Kai-shek. I have spoken to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon), and he has kindly consented to second a motion to this end. I therefore move, seconded by Mr. Graydon:
That the address of Madame Chiang Kai-shek, delivered before the members of the Senate and of the House of Commons of Canada in the chamber of the House of Commons this morning, and the record of the morning's proceedings, be included in the House of Commons Debates and form part of the records of this parliament.

The labour priorities schedule is continually being reviewed and revised by an informal interdepartmental committee of representatives of the wartime prices and trade board, the Department of Munitions and Supply and national selective service. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minutes of the meetings of the national finance committee which took place in Ottawa on December 9, 1936, and the following days, under

National Finance Committee
the chairmanship of the Minister of Finance were understood to be for the guidance and information of the members of the committee only, and not to be made public.
I have here the first volume of the minutes, and I would quote a few lines from it to bear out my statement:
Hon. Mr. Duplessis: This is a family gathering. We should keep our meetings closed, unless 'he committee decides otherwise.
Hon. Mr. Dunning:	We cannot of course
prevent the press from stating what they want to state. The object of having a stenographic report is solely for the convenience of members of this committee, after they return home. It cannot, of course, be completely typed while each meeting is on.
The procedure and the rule agreed on at that meeting was the same as that agreed on at other meetings, several of which were held, between the Minister of Finance and the provincial treasurers. On no occasion, so far as I can ascertain or recollect, were the minutes regarded as anything other than a record for the convenience of the persons who attended the conference. Indeed it was agreed at the meetings that they were not to be made public, but that press statements were to be given out following each meeting. Under those conditions I must take exception to the production of minutes on this motion. If the hon. member would like to have the press statements, which I presume are not adequate for his purposes, there would be no objection to trying to get them together and producing them. But I must take the position, in view of the arrangement with the provinces, thoroughly understood and agreed upon, that the minutes themselves are not producible.
I would point out to the Minister of Finance that having quoted from a public document such as this-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not a public document.
Oh, yes.
Just a minute; I have not finished.
It is official.

In any event it is an official document, and in my opinion comes within the rule which states that when any part of a document such as this has been quoted from the whole document must be tabled. Whatever grounds the minister had to sustain his objection are, I suggest, now swept from under him. I think the minister must now table the document.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend is raising a point in the nature of a technicality.
The rules cannot be interpreted as technicalities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It must be obvious that in the conduct of public business unless some documents may be regarded as confidential by the ministry it would not be possible on many occasions to have brought out the full information the government may wish to secure. Many statements are made in much greater detail by those giving information when it is known that their statements will be protected, or where it is certain-or even uncertain-that the documents themselves containing these statements may not be called for. I know what the rules are, and my hon. friend, does too. But in this instance I submit it is quite clear, from the minister's statement, that the document should not be tabled, and I hope my hon. friend will not press the objection he has raised, one which I think really is more in the nature of a technical objection.

I wish to thank the Prime Minister at least for having confirmed my position with respect to the rules of the house. I should not like him to take the position that by urging that the rules of the house be followed one is raising an undue technicality. As I see it, the rules of the house can scarcely be placed in that category. The Prime Minister also implied that the information furnished would contain what the members of the committee may have said. My reading of the suggested order is that it calls for a copy of the minutes and report of the meetings of the national finance committee. I submit that is a long way from tabling the transcript of evidence showing what had actually happened. This asks for minutes, and I think they come within an entirely different category.
I still urge that the Minister of Finance might have been on safer ground if he had used a different objection. May I add that on one or two other occasions in the house the government has offered similar grounds for refusing to produce reports. Perhaps on those occasions the grounds were not quite as poor as those we have heard to-day. Nevertheless I say the house and the public are entitled to the fullest information respecting matters of this kind. Surely there cannot be anything extremely confidential in national war savings committee minutes. That committee deals with a matter of major importance, namely the financing of part of Canada's war commitments. With due deference for the Prime Minister's position, I hope he will not press the technicality on that.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INAUGURATION OF AVAR SERVICE FOR MAILS AND PASSENGERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to inform the house regarding the establishment of a transatlantic air service. Arrangements have been completed for the immediate establishment of a Canadian government war-time transatlantic air service to carry mail to and from the Canadian armed forces in the British isles and to transport members of the Canadian armed forces and of Canadian government departments and technicians engaged in the production of war materials. The new war service is not a commercial or a permanent one. It will carry no fare-paying passengers. Space on the aircraft from Canada will be

Labour Conditions-War Workers
allocated by the deputy minister of transport in Ottawa; space on aircraft westward by the Canadian high commissioner in London.
The growing strength of the Canadian armed forces overseas and their increasing activities have made it necessary to establish this quick and effective means of communication with the United Kingdom for men and materials. The need for a speedy and regular troops air mail service is particularly pressing. Over a quarter of a million members of the Canadian armed forces are now in the United Kingdom. During the past year, due to lack of space on aircraft, they have unfortunately not been receiving mail regularly and quickly. It is expected that the initial flight of the new service will occur early in July.

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, June 15, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to his majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the Chair.

['Madame Chiang Kai-shek, I would seek to convey what has been made so manifest by this audience during your address-the deep sense of gratitude that you have evoked by your message, and the privilege which is ours to have heard not only the voice of China, but the voice of freedom, expressed by you in most eloquent terms and phrased in graceful English, comparable with the best in our literature. I speak not for both houses of parliament alone, but for all Canada, when I express the profound admiration of its citizens for Chung Hua Min Kou, or in our language, literally meaning "Chinese People's Country", the lovely name of the new China. And if I may be permitted to say, you have captivated all our hearts.

Questions
Your country has furnished great gifts to the world and when the time comes, as it surely will, when those evil people shall be driven from your land, China will once again take pride in its ancient culture and appease its hunger and thirst for the new learning in the new schools and colleges which, even in the midst of universal destruction, your people have built.
May I respectfully request, Madame, that you will as opportunity offers, convey to your noble and heroic husband, Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, Canada's abiding sense of obligation to him and to his valiant people. Canada's war is in the Orient as well as in Europe. Our armed forces are now fighting with your armed forces against Japan, and neither Canada nor China will lay down arms until they exact the unconditional surrender of that country.
It is for the good of all mankind that your and our race and peoples should understand and share friendship. May God in His infinite wisdom sustain and preserve you, and on that glorious day when this war shall cease, Canada will gladly join with your people in their long awaited triumph and will joyously repeat with you: Forever China.
Madame, on behalf of Canada I say: We thank you.
The National Anthem having been sung, the gathering dispersed with three cheers for Madame Chiang Kai-shek.
Thursday, June 17, 1943']

I was asked to give a statement of the reasons for selection of petroleum instead of alcohol as the base for the production of synthetic rubber. As hon. members know, the rubber crisis came on us very suddenly. At the fall of Singapore, or when Singapore was threatened we had occasion for the first time to be concerned about, our stocks of rubber. Fortunately we had fairly large stocks on hand, and even larger stocks on order. When the fall of Singapore occurred we had some 21,000 tons in Singapore and Penang. Of course we gave that up for lost, but strangely enough, practically all of that rubber arrived in Canada in due course, some of it after months. One boat had been in Penang harbour loading when the attack on Penang harbour came; it arrived months later with something like thirty or forty shell holes in the hull. It limped along without communicating with anyone and worked its way back into Halifax harbour. That, as I remember it, was a boat owned by the Canadian National Steamships. Other rubber was put on small boats, any sort of craft, and sent to any destination, but it was all billed to Canada and eventually practically all of it found its way here. However, we had to take immediate stock of the situation, and if we were to continue to play a useful part in the war we had to take immediate steps to find a substitute for natural rubber. Our neighbours to the south were in the same position. We pooled our stocks of rubber and we pooled the information as to the best move to make to meet the situation when existing stocks of rubber were to be exhausted. It was decided by consultations in which the best technical men of the United States, joined with the best technical men of Canada, that the only satisfactory sub-
War Appropriation-Supplies

stitute for natural rubber is the type of rubber known as buna-S rubber. It is a compound of two elements, butadiene and styrene. The process is first of producing the two elements that make up that rubber, and then for polymerizing the two into artificial rubber. The best industrial engineers in the United States were engaged to engineer the necessary plans. Arrangements were made that all patents held in the United States for the process would be pooled and made free to both governments for the duration of the war and a certain period thereafter. It was the combined judgment of the two countries that petroleum as a base for butadiene would be the cheapest and most satisfactory.
At the time the decision had to be made, most of the United States programme for production of buna-S synthetic rubber was predicated on use of petroleum as a base stock for the production of butadiene. In order to get the project under way with minimum delay, as part of the over-all north American programme and obtain the necessary priority ratings for equipment and materials which were not procurable from Canadian sources, it was considered1 advisable to use existing plans, designs, drawings and specifications which had been prepared and developed by the Rubber Reserve Company of the United States.
Extensive development work in the processes involved in the production of butadiene from a petroleum base had been made in the United States, and Canada was offered the use of all information obtained on the same basis as similar projects in the United States.
Canada was given the full benefit of the patent pooling agreements which had been made by the Rubber Reserve company with the companies and industries in the United States whom it was felt were best qualified to help the government overcome the intricate problems which arose out of the manufacture of synthetic rubber on the large scale required for the war programme for the united nations. Under these agreements the processes covered by the valuable patents owned by the Standard Oil Development company covering the manufacture of buna-S and butyl rubber and butadiene, the principal basic material in the manufacture of buna-S, became royalty free for the period of the emergency. A certain percentage-25 per cent-of the materials and equipment required was not obtainable from Canadian sources, and by following the United States programme Canada was able to obtain much specially designed equipment by merely placing duplicating orders with the fabricators. In fact the main Canadian plants are duplicates of the corresponding United States plants.

We had at that time no other choice than to go to the United States for the engineering ability and technical skill required in the construction of the necessary plants, and the engineering firms whose services were available were mainly engaged on the petroleum base process.
The main decision made in Canada was to erect a plant capable of producing 34,000 long tons of buna-S per annum and the two basic materials required for its manufacture, namely, butadiene and styrene. Butadiene could be produced either from alcohol or from a petroleum base. The survey showed:
(a)	That the total facilities for the production of alcohol in Canada would produce less than one-third of the alcohol that would be required to provide the butadiene equivalent of the rubber required for the Canadian war programme.
(b)	That the combined cost of building additional facilities for the production of alcohol and the cost of building plants for the manufacture of butadiene from alcohol, were greater than the costs of building a plant capable of producing a similar quantity of butadiene from petroleum.
(c)	That in the cracking processes involved in recovering butadiene from petroleum we could recover ethylene, the principal basic material required for the manufacture of styrene, and could also recover isobutylene, the very cheap basic material used in the manufacture of butyl rubber.
(d)	That we could procure the butadiene, ethylene and isobutylene required for the production of 34,000 long tons of buna rubber and 7,000 long tons of butyl rubber without materially detracting from our normal gasoline and oil supplies.
It is generally assumed, I think, that by using an oil base for the production of rubber, the oil so used must be subtracted from the oil available for other purposes in Canada. That is not correct. The part of the oil that is used consists of the lighter fractions that are taken off in the cracking process, and after the requirements of rubber have been obtained there is just as good fuel oil left from the petroleum as would have been obtainable had the lighter fractions not been taken from the oil. The only difference that may be noted in the oil, after the light fractions have been taken out, is that it may not be quite as active in starting a car. The lighter fractions help to liven up the oil in starting a car, but apart from that there is just as good a product, practically as good a gasoline.

(e)	That we had in Canada an oil refinery fed by pipe line which would enable us to centralize the operations in one point and be assured of continuous production, whereas production of butadiene and styrene from an alcohol base would be contingent upon having a ready supply of tankers and tank cars.
The projected plan provided a self-contained economical and efficient operation for the following reasons:
(a)	The best available location selected provided an adequate area adjacent to one of the largest refineries in Canada, served by water, rail and highway transportation and at a relatively short distance from the plants of the Canadian rubber industry engaged in the production of tires, which will consume about 85 per cent of the synthetic rubber to be produced.
How does rubber made from butyl compare with regular rubber in mileage and speed?

The last word about buna-S is not known. It has been produced for only a very short time. Intensive experiments are now going forward and various fabrics are being experimented with but it is believed, from tests made to date, that buna-S rubber with nylon fabric will make a tire that is at least ninety-five per cent as long-lived as the best tire from natural rubber, and it is believed that with further experimentation and the further development of the art a better tire can be produced from buna-S rubber than can be made from the natural product.
Forty miles an hour would be quite safe?

Oh, yes; it is a first-class tire.
(b)	By extending the cracking facilities of one of the largest refineries in the country, we could obtain the desired quantities of three gases for which a limited use had previously been found, namely, ethylene, isobutylene and butylene, on a relatively low cost basis.
(c)	By erecting styrene, butyl and buna-S copolymer plants nearby, these gases can be transferred by pipeline without the costs, complications, difficulties and dangers involved in their transportation by tank cars.
The problems of developing organizations to produce synthetic rubber in satisfactory amounts and qualities and of procuring or training the necessary operating personnel for the various plants in the Canadian project could, for obvious reasons, best be met and solved by following the main lines of the United States programme.
The production of butadiene from a petroleum base did not preclude the possibility of using an alcohol base at some subsequent date, should it be found economical or advisable to do so, but at the present time the low cost of producing butadiene from butane, derived in the oil cracking process, as compared with its cost of production from grain definitely rules out the latter.
It is estimated that the cost of conversion alone in the production of industrial alcohol is approximately 10 cents to 12 cents per gallon from grain. Taking grain at, say, 80 cents a bushel, the cost of production for industrial alcohol from grain would run from 50 cents to 60 cents a gallon. If industrial alcohol is produced from whisky distilleries, the cost may range over 80 cents per gallon. For instance, in order to get our styrene plant into production as early as possible, we have found it advisable to purchase a limited quantity of ethyl alcohol for this purpose. The cost of this material laid down at the plant is 88 cents per gallon and, according to our information, this high cost will have the effect of increasing the cost of finished styrene by about 1,000 per cent. It is estimated that a United States gallon of alcohol yields approximately 2-2 pounds of butadiene and that the theoretical yields of butadiene from alcohol and butane respectively are 59 per cent and 93 per cent by weight, and that the cost of producing butane from industrial alcohol is about three times the cost of production from butane.
In order to equalize these costs, the purchase price of grain would have to be 25 cents to 30 cents per bushel. This is, perhaps, one of the reasons the farm bloc in the United States is not pressing further for the use of grain in the production of butane. Under present conditions it can be applied to many other purposes which will yield the farmer a much higher price.
That is the whole story about the use of wheat for industrial purposes. It can be used for the manufacture of rubber and for other industrial purposes, but to be used in competition with other available substances it must be sold at a very low price, and I am sure no hon. member would wish to encourage the use of wheat which would be predicated on a cost at point of use of from 25 cents to 30 cent a bushel.
In considering Canada's project for the provision of buna-S and butyl synthetic rubbers, it should be borne in mind at all times that the Canadian government owns and controls (a) the plant investment; (b) the operation of the plants and (c) the products and by-products

I shall be glad to do so, if I can obtain unanimous consent, and if the king's printer does not object. The statement is as follows:
Comments in regard to the charges, accusations and statements made by one, Dyson Carter, in a publication entitled, "So That Man May Prosper".
The main theme contained in the publication seems to be as follows:
Since butadiene, one of the principal materials required in the production of buna-S rubber, can be produced, either from alcohol or petroleum, and that since we have a surplus supply of grain, Canada has made a grave mistake in deciding to manufacture butadiene from a petroleum base instead of using its surplus grain for the production of .this material. That by using a petroleum base, we are unnecessarily consuming valuable supplies of crude oil when we need to make every barrel of crude petroleum available for war purposes. That ds the capital cost involved and the material required in the construction of plants to produce butadiene from petroleum is greatly in excess of the cost and quantity of materials and equipment required to produce it from alcohol obtained from grain; and further, that these grain alcohol plants can be constructed immediately in the large wheat growing areas of the country to produce synthetic rubber from wheat as a vital war production measure.
He states that we could produce cheaper rubber by using the alcohol-from-grain process because there are several such processes now "in the course of development" which will lower the cost of production and may be subsequently further improved.
The author of this publication has obviously made considerable study of the subject, but all through the piece he has the habit of jumping to erroneous conclusions and then building up a story of a false hypothesis. In spite of his expressed effort to get at the bottom of the subject and the true facts, he does not appear to have taken the trouble to inquire from any officials of the Department of Munitions and Supply, or of the Polymer Corporation Limited, a crown company formed for the purpose of constructing, equipping and operating a series of Canadian government-owned plants to produce synthetic rubber, as to the basic principles underlying the project or the reasons why they were followed. If he had done so, he would have had to revise a considerable portion of his booklet.
One is inclined to suspect that he was more interested in creating an alarming story which would appeal to sectional prejudice and substantially increase the sale of his publication, than in an accurate presentation of the actual situation. In the course of the article, he raises certain questions and makes an abnormally large number of insidious references for the apparent purpose of leading the Canadian public to believe that the petroleum interests, in both Canada and the U.S., are attempting to secure a monopoly on our synthetic rubber business by what he terms "racketeering and profiteering methods".

<b) The capital costs are about one-half as much for crop-rubber plants as for petroleum rubber plants.
(c)	No one knows the large-scale plant operating cost for producing rubber by any process. According to the best estimates agricultural products appear to be fully competitive with petroleum.
(d)	The only known-to-be-successful synthetic rubber plants in Europe are based on agricultural crops.
Would the minister comment upon this statement by the Doan agricultural service?

I can only repeat that it is the quickest way to get butadiene, starting from scratch. WTe examined the cost of
facilities very carefully, and, assuming that you must/build a plant to make ethyl alcohol, and convert that ethyl alcohol into butyl alcohol, and then into butadiene, we found it a more expensive operation than building a plant to make butadiene from petroleum. A very careful analysis made by the best experts I could obtain in Canada-and including experts associated *with our national research council-is that it is competitive, provided wheat can be bought at the plant for from 25 to SO cents a bushel.
The butadiene to be made in the plant at Sarnia is to be from oil.
Yes, that is correct.
And the styrene also is to be made from oil

One small component of styrene, namely ethylene, may be obtained from the same cracking process which makes butadiene. But the principal ingredients of styrene are, I believe, a by-product of the coke-from-gas industry and are transported from Hamilton.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the minister would make any further answers he wishes to make with respect to rubber.

If there is to be any further debate in respect of rubber, then it might be well to finish it now. If we can confine ourselves to a discussion of rubber, I shall be glad to answer any other questions.

What proposals or schemes are there for the disposal of these plants after the war? I have in mind the Sarnia plant, for instance, and other additions. In the course of his remarks he said that the Sarnia plant, with perhaps extensions or additions, might be sufficient for peace-time needs. I think we should know now what is planned in that connection. It must have been canvassed and considered, otherwise the minister would not have been in a position to make that statement. I have reasons for asking this question, because, in addition to the fact that the government is advancing from $40,000,000 to $50,000,000 to this plant, the people of Canada have a right to know now the government's policy in respect to these plants. I realize an opportunity has not yet been given to the minister to reply to certain questions I asked the other day. I believe the rubber question might be separated from questions connected with government advances to other corporations. I say that because a few nights ago the hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Bence) referred to a statement

War Appropriation-Supplies
made by a consulting chemist of the Dow Chemical company. That statement has received wide circulation and to my knowledge has never been denied or answered by any governmental authority either in Canada or the United States. The statement was made last February before the Minnesota bankers' association, and was to the effect that the outstanding reason for not proceeding with the production of rubber through the use of alcohol manufactured from wheat, and the like, was that some arrangement had been made between the oil companies and the united nations with south African countries, whereby provision was being made now, or had been made under unpublicized treaties, for the destruction of all United States synthetic rubber plants after the conclusion of the war. That has been given wide publicity. According to the minister it will require considerable expenditure to produce rubber from an alcohol base; nevertheless it would build up an industry in war time which would be beneficial in peace time and give Canada an opportunity to dispose of her surplus wheat. Is there any foundation for the statements made by this gentleman? What are the official plans for the disposal of these rubber plants? Does the government intend to turn them over to private industry, or does the government intend to operate them as government enterprises after the war?

I read the statement of the man who my hon. friend says is an official of the Dow Chemical company. I do not believe he is an outstanding official of that company.
Mr. DIEFENBAKEIt: He is a research consultant.

He is not an executive of the company; he is a research consultant. I was consultant to a great many firms, and I presume this gentleman is a consultant to the Dow company and many others. I do not think it is the duty of a public man to deny everything he reads in the papers, especially statements by a man he never heard of. I have said already that the plant at Sarnia is exclusively the property of the government of Canada; it will be operated by the government of Canada; its products will be at the disposal of the government of Canada; they will be owned by the government of Canada and will be sold in the interests of the government of Canada. So far as I know that situation will continue indefinitely. I know of no change that is contemplated. Governments come and go and policies change with different governments. What the next government will do, I do not
know, but it is the intention of this government to continue to operate the plant at Sarnia to make rubber for the country at war and the country at peace.
Do I understand the minister to say that alcohol made from wheat costing SI per bushel will cost something in the neighbourhood of 75 to 80 cents a gallon?
At the distillery.
In normal times alcohol is made from molasses?
Yes.
For about what price?
I think 25 cents is a good price for alcohol in peace time, although it may be less.
I understand that it could be made in peace time for about 15 to 20 cents.
While it may not be the custom of the minister to deny what appears in the press, has he any knowledge of any such treaty?
No.

The minister has just said that the plant at Sarnia is being operated by the government and that it is the intention of the government, at present at any rate, to continue to operate it. A few minutes ago the minister tabled certain orders in council which have to do with the plant at Sarnia. Some weeks ago these orders and some others were tabled in response to a question of mine. I have not that sessional paper here, but my recollection of the situation, after studying those orders in council, is that the government owns the Polymer Corporation and that the government, through the minister, appointed the directors who are in charge of the plant on behalf of the government. I understand that they serve without fee. As I recall the orders in council, these directors have reported back to the government from time to time and have made certain recommendations. I think it was in April of this year that the directors recommended that the operation of this plant should be turned over to Imperial Oil and its subsidiaries. As I say, I am speaking from memory. Perhaps I should have said that the directors recommended that this government owned company ask Imperial Oil and some of its subsidiaries to come in and operate the plant. Some of us have the fear -the minister may not like our being suspicious in this way-that if Imperial Oil is called in to operate this plant during the
War Appropriation-Supplies

course of the war, when the war is over Imperial Oil will be the only ones who really know anything about it. There would then be a very good chance of their getting control of the plant, unless steps are taken now to guarantee that it will continue as a government owned and government operated plant. I shall be glad if the minister will correct me if my story is not correct.

The cracking process for
making butadiene requires oil technicians. Imperial Oil are represented on the board of a company subsidiary to Polymer which is in charge of that operation. The officers of that company and the employees of that company are on the government payroll. Imperial Oil is assisting the government to get that branch of the business under way. Naturally you cannot pick men off the street who know how to crack oil to get the light fractions such as are used to produce butadiene. Imperial Oil are furnishing certain technical assistants, but they are doing it for government account.
Are those men on leave of absence?

They are engaged by the
government. Many men have come there direct from the universities to be trained, and they are government employees. The Dow Chemical company, who are experts in the production of styrene, are sponsoring operations at this plant in a similar way. They are furnishing the technical experts and have designed that section of the plant. They are training government employees in the manufacture of styrene. The four rubber companies which are the principal users of the product of this plant for the manufacture of tires and other products have joined together to take over the direction of a subsidiary company of Polymer which is operating the polymerization plant. Here again the employees are government employees, the rubber companies simply giving technical assistance to that branch of the enterprise. I may say that the Polymer corporation, which is a wholly government owned corporation-
Is that at Sarnia?

The whole operation is at Sarnia. The Polymer corporation owns the property, is responsible for the operations, and will be responsible for the sale of the product. It is a government owned corporation, responsible to the government.
What are the relationships between the other companies referred to and Imperial Oil? The St. Clair Processing company was one, I think.

That is the subsidiary of
Imperial which at the moment is responsible for the operation of the butadiene end.
I believe another one is the Canadian Synthetic Rubber company.
That is the subsidiary formed by the rubber companies to assist the government in the polymerization process.
As I understand it, these companies have lent the government certain technicians.
That is right.
And the government has taken into these plants a number of young scientists from the universities who are being trained as technicians.
That is right.

If I understand aright there will be a competent staff trained by the technicians which in the event of the country desiring to continue the operation of this plant, apart from Imperial Oil or the Dow Chemical company, will be available.
Oh, yes.
I am glad to get that assurance from the minister.

Many of us are intensely interested in the experimental work being carried on to produce alcohol from wheat. I have read from time to time that certain distilleries, particularly the larger ones, have been carrying on this kind of experimental work. Has that work been done with or without government financial assistance? If with government financial assistance, under what terms and conditions is the assistance given? Can the minister tell us what quantity of Canadian wheat was used last year in the production of alcohol?

Experiments have been carried on both by the distilleries and by scientific laboratories. Ontario government laboratories and our own national research laboratories have conducted quite extensive experiments in converting alcohol into butyl alcohol. I think that the experiments by the distilleries have been conducted at their own expense. It is pointed out by all that it is a difficult process. The bug that operates on wheat to convert it into butyl alcohol is a very delicate creature requiring great quantities of stainless steel to house the process. At one stage we tried to get the distilleries to make butyl alcohol with their present equipment but were assured that they could not do so and that

War Appropriation-Supplies
reconstruction of the distilleries would be necessary to convert wheat directly into butyl alcohol suitable for butadiene.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister deserves a good deal of credit for what he has already done in trying to bring about the production of rubber in Canada. I am going to ask him to go one step further and during the time that the whole process is under construction, and after it is in operation, to have government auditors make a survey of the exact cost of each process which enters into the construction of rubber in Canada. There is no certainty that after the war we shall be able to obtain raw rubber from Malaya. We read quite frequently that just before the Japs are kicked out of Malaya they will destroy the rubber forests. I hope that will not be so, but they may do that, in which case we shall not be able to obtain rubber from that source. The government is now financing rubber factories, I presume at very heavy cost-I am not blaming the government for that-and that is why I make this suggestion. I am informed by a steam-fitting company which I have known for many years that during the erection of the plant in Sarnia pipe-fitters had to be brought from across the line. That may or may not be so; I do not know. But I was told that these pipe-fitters were paid a very high wage or salary and were paid in United States money, or in Canadian money plus the exchange. I asked how much they drew and I was told that one man drew over S180 in one week for pipefitting. That might have included overtime and everything else. Naturally the minister would want to have this plant in operation in the shortest possible time, and to do that the men would have to work overtime. Therefore I am not blaming the minister for the high costs. But assuming that the costs were high, I hope that a careful check will be made by auditors so that if it is necessary for Canada after the war to keep these plants in operation our own tire factories may be supplied with rubber at a price which the government itself will know is reasonable. I am in favour of private industry because I believe that private industry will produce goods at less cost than the government can. Private industry runs its business on a business-like basis. Governments cannot. They have to stick this man in here and that man in there, and that cannot be avoided. But if a careful audit is made of those plants which may continue to produce rubber after the war Canadians will not have to pay too much for the rubber we need.
The more I look into it the more I am amazed at the phenomenal capacity of the
Germans in invention. If they had only used their great brains for the world's good, instead of, as they were, producing and inventing for war purposes, how much better it would have been for themselves and for the world! I believe it was Doctor ter Meer who discovered the process of making butadiene from oil. He had his process well developed by the early twenties, at which time Germany was producing oil from coal. It is amazing to me what a long line of products Germany has produced from coal, not only rubber, oil, and explosives-I believe toluol, which forms a basis of TNT, has been produced from coal- but several other products. The German government discovered that rubber could be made from coal through chemical processes, and then what did they do? They brought about the erection of a plant in 1937 to produce 30,000 tons of rubber a year. Another plant was erected in 1939 to produce 30,000 tons of rubber a year, and another of the same capacity was erected in 1940. They were setting out to destroy the world. That was the motive behind their inventions. I think in peace time we can make good use of these inventions.
I should like to find out from the minister what is the connection between those who are producing rubber, or the basis of rubber, at Sarnia and the Standard Oil company. The Standard Oil company owns the patents for America of the process. If on account of the war they are not charging for the use of these patents any more than the mere cost to themselves, that is all right; but if they are charging exorbitant prices for the use of these patents we should know it. They put up a pilot plant at Baton Rouge, and, according to evidence given before a committee of the United States senate, were producing by 1941 eighteen tons of butadiene per day; that is really 7,000 tons a year. On the basis of their costs in their pilot plant at Baton Rouge they took a contract from the United States government to supply 40,000 tons at 13-6 cents per pound. I should like to know what is the difference between the cost of butadiene per pound and of the finished rubber per pound. Then I should like to know if the government is keeping accurate audited costs of these plants that are being erected, and if it proposes to keep accurate costs of the finished rubber per pound produced by the goverment plants, so that the Canadian people will be defended against exploitation after the war and rubber will be sold at the right price. Because I am of the opinion that if the Japanese destroy the rubber forests of Malaya before they retire from that country-as we hope they will be forced to do-our Sarnia plant will prove a great advantage to Canada and incidentally bring

War Appropriation-Supplies
much credit to the industry for having erected it there. The butyl, of course, is made from alcohol and can be made from oil of coal.

No, it is not made from
alcohol. That is, it will not be so made here.

The Germans say it
can be.
Yes, it can be.

I agree with what has been said, and I close by expressing the hope that if after the war Canada is compelled to manufacture synthetic rubber from either buna-S or butyl, the minister-and if he undertakes to do it nothing will stop him- w'ill thoroughly consider what has been suggested, and what I have suggested before, that a plant be put up in the west to produce butyl from alcohol. It is the duty of us all to try to free the west from the unhappy consequences of the depression. If a small plant could be established there to use 25 or 50 million bushels of wheat a year in the development of butyl for the production of rubber, we are in duty bound to assist the west to that extent. Certainly the plant at Sarnia will have all it can do to take care of eastern requirements.
I should like the minister to say whether records have been kept as to the cost in advance, to protect the future selling price of rubber to the Canadian people, and I should like to know about what time Canadian users of tires may hope to be able to buy tires made at the plant at Sarnia.

Most careful accounts are being kept of the expenditures. Both the Polymer company and the treasury have cost accountants on the work at the present time. Of course this is an expensive period to build anything, but I think, having that in mind the plant is being built economically. I know of no pipefitters being brought across the line. The Dow Chemical company, our engineers on the styrene plant, may have brought across' a few expert foremen, to handle the piping. As my hon. friend knows, a chemical plant consists almost wholly of high pressure piping; it is a specialist's task, and I am not saying that men may not have been brought across the line, though I have no knowledge of it. The wages paid at Sarnia are the wages set by the Department of Labour for the various trades; so far as I know they apply to all the employees on the job. The cost of building at the present time is higher than the cost of budding in peace time; how much higher, I cannot say. This is specialized work: every piece of material in the plant 
has to be specially designed and built. I will say this, we shall try to produce rubber at a competitive price, and as a government operation. If there is no other rubber about, it might be good business for the government to sell at a competitive price in any event, whether it can be produced at a competitive price or not; that is a matter for the future.
I have given a lot of study to the manufacture of synthetic rubber and I am confident that we are building an industry which will be effective in peace time as well as during the war. It may not be producing exactly the article that is produced to-day. But when we cast our minds over the great list of products made to-day from the light fractions of petroleum-items of great use in our civilization-I am certain that we are not building a plant at Sarnia with any prospect it wdl be closed when the war is finished or when natural rubber comes back into free supply from other countries.

After the war how will the government or the Canadian people be protected against any exorbitant price which might be charged by Standard Oil-I do not say that they will attempt to impose one- for the processes used in the production of rubber? The company control absolutely the hydrogenation process and the catalytic cracking process, and anyone wishing to produce rubber will have to obtain, the right from the Standard Oil, because they received it under the Hague convention of 1939 and they promised to hand it out. But shall we be protected from an exorbitant price for their process?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. All the patents having to do with the manufacture of butyl rubber or buna-S rubber have been pooled with the United States government, and Canada has been included to share with the United States the right to these patents. I would not care to give the house the exact terms, but they are the same for Canada as for all plants being built for the United States government. My recollection is that no royalty is payable during the war and for a certain period thereafter, and that after that there is a royalty payable which has been agreed upon by the United States, by the subsidiaries, and by Canada.
Per pound?

I could not say. I do not recall the terms of the agreement, but we have an agreement. It is the same agreement as the United States government has, covering the patents of this process for peacetime use.

War Appropriation-Supplies

I should like to refer for a moment or two to the question of the operation of the plant at Sarnia. We were discussing it a short while ago, and the minister and I differed as to the terms of the order in council, which neither of us had before him at the time. I have since looked into the matter, and I have before me a copy of the order in council to which I referred and a copy of the other orders in council dealing with this matter. In P.C. 2799, April 8, 1943, there appears, after the statement that the committee of the privy council have before them the report of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, the following:
That the company reports that
(b) Arrangements have been made with Imperial Oil Limited and its subsidiary, St. Clair Processing Corporation Limited, Dow Chemical Company of Canada Limited, and Canadian Synthetic Rubber Limited, for the operation of the respective units being constructed.
I am alarmed at the wording of a previous order in council, P.C. 2369, of March 27, 1942, which was the order in council that set up the Polymer Corporation Limited, setting out its general terms. Part of the order in council is schedule A, the memorandum of agreement, in which we are advised regarding the functions of the Polymer Corporation Limited. I read, in section 1, subsection (a):
The company will forthwith proceed to acquire, construct, instal and establish the necessary land, buildings, machinery, equipment and plant . . . for the manufacture, production and storage of synthetic rubber.
I call attention to the significant omission from this original order in council of the word operation. Polymer Corporation Limited was set up to acquire, construct, instal and establish the plant, but no mention is made that Polymer corporation, which is owned by the government, should operate the plant. Then thirteen months later the company recommends to the government that the companies which I have named should operate the respective units being con-constructed, and P.C. 2799, of April 8, 1943, approves the recommendation that these companies operate the plant.
Another sessional paper, which was brought down in response to questions of mine, gives us the names of the president, the vicepresident, the managing director and the directors of Polymer Corporation Limited. They are:	R. C. Berkinshaw, President;
D. W. Ambridge, Vice-President; J. R. Nicholson, Managing Director; W. R. Campbell, A. C. Guthrie, A. J. Crawford, G. A. LaBine, and Colonel A. L. Bishop, directors.
I will not read in full sessional paper No. 388, to which I am referring, but it shows that these men I have named hold the offices indicated, and that many of them are directors of other companies. It is the usual who's who of big business, and here again is the story of a group-
What big business is Mr. Crawford in?

Well, since the minister has asked I will give the details:
R. C. Berkinshaw is general manager and treasurer of the Goodyear Tire and Rubber Co. of Canada Limited. He is a director of the following firms or corporations:	Goodyear
Cotton Co. of Canada Ltd.; Toronto Elevators Limited (vice-president); Easy Washing Machine Co.: Ltd. (vice-president); Crown Trust Company; Polymer Corporation Limited; Mutual Life Assurance Co. of Canada.
D. W. Ambridge is assistant general manager of the Ontario Paper Company and is now on loan to the Department of Munitions and Supply as director general, naval shipbuilding branch. He is a director of the following firms or corporations: Polymer Corporation Limited (vice-president); Best Yeast Company.
Wallace R. Campbell is president, treasurer and director of the Ford Motor Company of Canada, Ltd. He is also a director of the following firms or corporations: Ford Motor Co. of Australia Pty. Ltd.: Ford Motor Co. of New Zealand Ltd.; Ford Motor Co. of South Africa Ltd.; Ford Motor Co. of India Ltd.; Ford Motor Co. of Malaya Ltd.; Polymer Corporation Limited.
A. C. Guthrie is president of Simmons Limited, Canada. He is a director of the following firms or corporations: Simmons Limited, Canada; Simmons Limited, U.S.A. and its subsidiaries (director and vice-president); The Murphy Paint Co. Limited, Montreal.
A. J. Crawford is employed by Sheet Metal Workers' International Association and as a director of Polymer Corporation. He represents the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. He is a director of no other firm or corporation.
G. A. LaBine is president of Eldorado Gold Mines Limited. He is also a director of the following firms or corporations:	Eldorado
Mining and Refining Limited; Gunnar Gold Mines Limited; Howey Gold Mines Limited; Pan-American League Against Cancer, Inc; member of the board of governors of the University of Toronto; Polymer Corporation Limited.
Col. A. L. Bishop is president of the Coniagas Mines Limited; Coniagas Reduction Co. Ltd.; Sturgeon River Gold Mines Limited and The Consumer Gas Co. of Toronto. He is a director of the following firms or corporations: Coniagas Mines Limited; Coniagas Reduction Co. Ltd.; Sturgeon River Gold Mines Ltd.; Consumer Gas Co. of Toronto; Coniaurum Mines Limited (vice-president); The Manufacturers Life Insurance Company; The Toronto General Trusts Corporation; Imperial Bank of Canada; Anglin Norcross Corporation Ltd.; Anglin Norcross (Ontario) Limited; Canadian General Investment Limited; Canadian Locomotive Co. Ltd.; Commonwealth Electric Corporation Limited;
War Appropriation-Supplies

The Consolidated Mining and Smelting Corporation of Canada; Toronto Shipbuilding Co. Ltd. (crown corporation).
J. R. Nicholson is managing director of Polymer Corporation Limited. Formerly Mr. Nicholson was deputy controller of supplies in the Department of Munitions and Supply. Other directorships-none.
I submit that, in the light of this information, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and I, though we may not want the same set-up after the war, are equally entitled to some more definite statement as to what is to happen to these plants at that time. I am not for the moment entering into a discussion of the merits of producing rubber from alcohol or oil, and I am not to be taken as at all deprecating the fact that a synthetic rubber plant is being built. All power to the minister in getting rubber produced. But I am concerned about the set-up which I have outlined. First, we have a company set up, and emphasis is placed on the fact that it is a completely government-owned company and that its directors serve without fee. But as you read the orders in council you discover that the company was given all the functions connected with getting the plant started but not the function of operating it, whereas thirteen months later the company, consisting of the directors whom I have just identified, recommends that the operation of the plant be carried on by the companies that I have named: Imperial Oil Limited and its subsidiary, St. Clair Processing Corporation Limited, Dow Chemical Company of Canada Limited and Canadian Synthetic Rubber Company Limited. Some of us have the genuine fear that when the war is over these are the companies which will be in virtual possession by reason of the fact that they will know how to operate the concern, and there is every possibility that what should continue as a government project after the war-that is just as important then as it is now-will pass out of the government's control.
Mr. HOWE; To me one of the discouraging features of public life is the objection that certain members have to using the experience of men who have gained that experience in the hard way and have emerged as successful men of business. I wonder who my hon. friend would choose to be directors of a great corporation responsible for spending some $40,000,000. I think each of us is wise to follow his own experience. I have been a professional man all my life. I have learned how to do certain things by doing them, and by doing them repeatedly. I have done more work, perhaps, in the building of grain ele-

vators than in any other branch of engineering, and I can tell my hon. friend that the last grain elevator I designed was vastly better than the first one; it was less costly to the owner and more efficient, and that was the result of my experience gained in doing the same work repeatedly.
When my hon. friend and various others rise in their places here and say we should have farmers, and we should have labour men, to direct these corporations, let me tell him that in the days of my private life farmers were my surest clients. The farmers do not do the things certain people in this house say we should do. When farmers spend the money of farmers, they choose men who have experience in doing the thing they want done. When the farmers wanted to build a terminal grain elevator they would come to me, because they knew I had built grain elevators, and they felt that I could give them value for their money. That is the view the farmers have taken; and I can tell you I admire them for the fact that any dollar they spend of cooperative money is well and carefully spent, under expert guidance. And they are not particular how much they pay for that expert guidance; they are willing to pay the current price in order to get the best advice available. That has been my experience in my own professional life, in spending the government's money. I have been spending other people's money for a great many years, and I know it has to be spent carefully. When I was made responsible for spending a few billion dollars belonging to the people of Canada, I got the very best advice I could get in the spending of that money. I have put in charge of every operation, for which I have been responsible to the people of Canada, the men best qualified by experience, and by having done similar work, to look after that operation. I am not apologizing to anyone in this house for having done that. It is all very well for a man of my hon. friend's experience to rise in his place here and sneer at people who occupy positions of trust in this country, but those are the people on whom I am banking. If I have made any success in handling my present portfolio, it is because I have been able to command the services and the devotion of those people in the job I have in hand. So that I wish my hon. friend would discontinue that line of cheap, soap-box oratory in this house.
On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, my remarks have been referred to as sneering. I wish to state to the minister that I have not objected to his-

No reply there.
